stem: A proposed AI use case cannot be sized in euros before work starts. What does the course recommend?

options.a: Do not start it: unsized gains are rarely captured
options.b: Run a pilot first, since the value will become clear
options.c: Size it after go-live, using real usage data
options.d: Use the vendor's ROI benchmark for similar sites

explanation: Approve AI work like capex: a euro figure, an owner and a stop date before any code. A gain that cannot be sized up front is rarely captured later.
author: claude-spec

stem: Scheduling software frees 3,000 hours a year. When do those hours become money?

options.a: As soon as the software goes live on the site
options.b: When the software licence has been fully paid off by the savings
options.c: When someone decides to fill them with orders or cut overtime
options.d: At the next annual budget review

explanation: Software frees capacity; only decisions turn it into money. Capture needs an owner with the mandate to take those decisions.
author: claude-spec

stem: Which gain counts as validated in the FDE School's sense?

options.a: Any gain the project team can model credibly
options.b: The output of the vendor's ROI calculator for the site
options.c: The projected gains of the next three sites in the planned rollout
options.d: A measurable, attributable gain signed off by client finance

explanation: A gain exists once the client's finance team signs it. Models, vendor calculators and pipeline do not count.
author: claude-spec

stem: Volume fell 15% after go-live and costs dropped. What stops your gains claim from counting the downturn?

options.a: Reporting only the first good month after go-live
options.b: A baseline normalized for volume and mix
options.c: Comparing against last year's best quarter
options.d: Keeping finance out of the review until the end

explanation: A gain is a difference against a baseline that moves with volume, mix and price: normalized baseline = baseline rate × actual volume, per family.
author: claude-spec

stem: Machine hours are freed in a plant that is not sold out. How should those hours be valued?

options.a: At the plant's full cost per machine-hour, overheads included
options.b: At the contribution margin of extra sales
options.c: At avoided variable cost, or via a structural decision
options.d: At the list price the vendor quotes for capacity

explanation: Contribution margin applies only when extra volume can actually be sold. Otherwise freed hours are worth avoided variable cost, or a structural move such as closing a shift, which management decides.
author: claude-spec

stem: Changeovers take 10,000 hours a year and a tool cuts them by 30%. Sold-out plant, €100 contribution per hour, software €100K a year. Net annual gain?
explanation: 3,000 freed hours × €100 = €300K gross, minus €100K of software = €200K net. €300K forgets the cost to achieve; €700K values the remaining hours; €1M forgets the 30%.
author: claude-spec

stem: Inventory falls by €2M after deployment. How should this appear in the gains case?

options.a: As €2M of recurring savings every year
options.b: One-time €2M cash release, plus recurring carrying-cost savings
options.c: Not at all, because inventory never appears anywhere on the P&L
options.d: As €400K of savings a year over five years

explanation: Cash release counts once as cash, and recurringly only as carrying cost. Presenting the one-time figure as annual savings destroys credibility with finance.
author: claude-spec

stem: Your teams submit 40 ideas for AI use cases. What does the course recommend doing with the list?

options.a: Fund a small pilot for each idea and keep the ones that seem to work
options.b: Rank the ideas by how quickly each one can be built
options.c: Keep the few that move margin, sized in euros; refuse most
options.d: Start with the ideas that have the most staff support

explanation: Start from the P&L: pick the few decisions that move margin and put a euro figure on each before any code. Piloting everything spreads effort over ideas that will never pay.
author: claude

stem: Polymex Industries can fund one AI project this year. Which target best fits the course's P&L-first approach?

options.a: Deciding the order sequence on the line that limits output
options.b: Summarizing meeting notes for every plant manager
options.c: A chatbot answering staff questions on HR policy
options.d: Helping the sales team write routine customer emails faster

explanation: The course targets the few decisions that move margin: what to schedule, buy, release or quote. Sequencing the line that limits output is one; the others save minutes, not margin.
author: claude

stem: Ferralux has €500M in revenue. A use case credibly promises one point of margin. How should its CEO read that?

options.a: About €50K a year: too small to matter
options.b: About €500K a year: fine for a local pilot
options.c: About €5M a year: worth changing how a plant works
options.d: About €50M a year: enough to fund a new plant

explanation: One point of margin on €500M is €5M a year, the scale the course considers worth changing how a plant works.
author: claude

stem: A vendor promises a 10% efficiency improvement on your scheduling. What is the course's view of that target?

options.a: Solid: any measurable gain is worth having
options.b: Too low: aim for multiples, since 10% rarely pays for the change
options.c: Acceptable, provided the vendor is willing to guarantee it in the contract
options.d: Good, as long as it shows within the first quarter

explanation: A 10% improvement rarely pays for the change it demands on the floor. Aim for multiples; a contract guarantee does not fix a target that is too small.
author: claude

stem: You report on the AI program to the board. Which figure should lead the report?

options.a: The number of AI use cases now live across sites
options.b: The share of staff who use AI tools every week
options.c: The hours saved, as reported by users in surveys
options.d: Euro gains signed off by the finance team

explanation: A gain exists only once the client's finance team signs it. Use cases live, usage and self-reported hours measure activity, not money.
author: claude

stem: A tool has freed hours on the line for six months, yet overtime spending has not moved. What is most likely missing?

options.a: More time for the tool to show its full results
options.b: Further training for staff on the tool's dashboards
options.c: A decision, by someone with the mandate, to cut the overtime
options.d: A more accurate and detailed model of machine capacity inside the tool

explanation: Software frees capacity; only decisions turn it into money. Waiting longer changes nothing if nobody decides to stop the overtime.
author: claude

stem: Your committee approves an AI project with a euro target and a named owner. Like any capex, what else must the approval set?

options.a: A date to stop it if the target is not in sight
options.b: A commitment to roll it out to every site afterwards
options.c: An open exploration budget for the first year
options.d: A shortlist of AI models to compare before starting

explanation: Approve AI projects like capex: a euro figure, an owner and a date to stop. Without a stop date, failing projects drift on.
author: claude

stem: After a year, 3 of your 10 AI initiatives have been stopped for missing their targets. How should the board read this?

options.a: As a sign the program is being poorly managed
options.b: As a reason to pause all new AI initiatives for at least a year
options.c: As proof the technology is not mature enough yet
options.d: As expected: about 30% fail, and stopping early is sound

explanation: The course expects about 30% of initiatives to fail and asks for them to be stopped early. A portfolio with no failures is usually not stopping anything.
author: claude

stem: At its review date, an AI initiative is clearly off its euro target, and the team asks for six more months. What does the course advise?

options.a: Stop it now and move the people to a better use case
options.b: Grant the extension, since AI projects need time to mature
options.c: Keep it running quietly without reporting the delay
options.d: Double the budget so it can reach the target faster

explanation: Some initiatives fail; the discipline is to stop them early. Extending a project that is clearly off target delays the inevitable and ties up scarce people.
author: claude

stem: Your CFO's AI case rests almost entirely on cutting operator headcount. What does the course expect to find?

options.a: That headcount is rightly where most of the value sits
options.b: That labor is usually a minority; bigger gains sit elsewhere
options.c: That no AI case should ever include labor savings
options.d: That headcount cuts are the quickest and easiest gains for finance to validate

explanation: Direct labor productivity is usually at most about a quarter of the value. Larger gains sit in working capital, speed to revenue, quality and deferred capex.
author: claude

stem: A tool frees a fifth of the planning team's time. One planner retires next month. What does the course suggest?

options.a: Hire a replacement quickly to keep the team at full strength
options.b: Wait a year before deciding anything about the team
options.c: Give the remaining planners more training on the tool
options.d: Do not replace the planner: that turns freed time into money

explanation: Freed time becomes money only through a decision, such as not replacing a leaver. Hiring a replacement quietly reabsorbs the gain.
author: claude

stem: How does the course recommend framing an AI gain when presenting it to plant teams?

options.a: As headcount the plant will be able to remove
options.b: As throughput: the same team producing more
options.c: As a percentage cut in the plant's labor cost
options.d: As hours each worker saves per week with the tool

explanation: Frame gains as throughput: the same team producing more. It matches where the value usually sits and does not turn the team against the tool.
author: claude

stem: Your team lists 'better visibility for planners' as a gain but cannot link it to any P&L line. How should the gains case treat it?

options.a: As a soft gain, valued at a share of planner salaries
options.b: As the main gain, since visibility drives all the others
options.c: As no gain until it branches to a financial line
options.d: As a gain counted once users confirm it in a survey

explanation: The gains tree runs from operational lever to physical effect to financial line. No branch to a P&L line, no gain.
author: claude

stem: A tool shortens changeovers. Which chain is a complete branch of the gains tree?

options.a: Shorter changeovers, a higher OEE score on the plant dashboard
options.b: Shorter changeovers, happier planners and better team morale on site
options.c: Shorter changeovers, fewer planner hours spent in spreadsheets
options.d: Shorter changeovers, more bottleneck output, margin on extra sales

explanation: A complete branch links lever, physical effect and financial line. A better OEE score is a physical effect that stops before reaching the P&L.
author: claude

stem: Demand at Polymex Industries is strongly seasonal. Which baseline period does the course call for?

options.a: The 3 months just before go-live
options.b: 12 rolling months
options.c: The 6 months of high season
options.d: The best single month of last year

explanation: With seasonality, the baseline covers 12 rolling months, never fewer than 6. A season-only window bakes the seasonal effect into the claimed gain.
author: claude

stem: Halfway through, the plant asks to add two new lines to the measured scope of the gains claim. What does baseline discipline require?

options.a: Keep the frozen, named perimeter; treat the new lines separately
options.b: Add them, and use the plant-wide average as their baseline
options.c: Add them, since a larger scope makes the claim more credible
options.d: Restart the whole baseline from scratch, including all of the lines

explanation: Baseline discipline means a frozen, named perimeter. Changing scope mid-way makes before and after incomparable; new lines need their own agreed baseline.
author: claude

stem: Resin prices fell 20% after go-live, cutting material costs. How should the gains claim treat this drop?

options.a: Count it, since it happened after the tool went live
options.b: Count half of it, as a compromise with finance
options.c: Normalize for price, so the drop is not claimed as a gain
options.d: Count it in full unless the controller can prove it came from elsewhere

explanation: The baseline is normalized for volume, mix and price. A market price drop is not caused by the tool, and claiming it destroys credibility with finance.
author: claude

stem: Of the four gain types, which carries the lightest burden of proof with finance?

options.a: Cost-out, such as an invoice that disappears
options.b: Revenue protection, such as a customer kept
options.c: Capacity release, such as machine hours freed
options.d: Cash release, such as inventory reduced

explanation: Cost-out is the easiest to validate. Capacity release needs the sold-out fork, cash release counts once, and revenue protection faces the most skepticism.
author: claude

stem: Your gains case says the tool prevented the loss of a major customer. What will finance need before counting it?

options.a: The sales team's estimate of how likely the loss was
options.b: A customer satisfaction survey run after go-live
options.c: The project team's model of churn risk across all customer accounts
options.d: Contractual evidence, such as penalty clauses

explanation: Revenue protection carries the highest skepticism and needs contractual evidence. Estimates, surveys and models are not proof that revenue was at risk.
author: claude

stem: Your plant is sold out and the tool frees bottleneck hours. Before valuing them at contribution margin, what must you obtain?

options.a: Confirmation from sales that the extra volume can be sold
options.b: The vendor's benchmark for freed capacity at similar sites
options.c: The full cost per machine-hour from the cost accounts
options.d: Agreement from the operators to work the freed hours

explanation: Capacity release becomes money at contribution margin only when sales confirm the extra volume can be sold. Full cost and vendor benchmarks do not prove it.
author: claude

stem: A new scheduler and a lean program both claim the same overtime reduction. What rule applies?

options.a: Each program counts the full reduction in its own case, as both helped
options.b: Count it once across both, allocated as agreed with finance
options.c: The program that started first counts all of it
options.d: Neither counts it, since attribution is impossible

explanation: Counting rules forbid double counting with other initiatives. The saving exists once; finance must see one figure, however it is shared.
author: claude

stem: Three months after go-live, the team reports the annualized run-rate as this year's savings. What is wrong?

options.a: Nothing, since run-rate is the standard way to report
options.b: Run-rate should be reported net of the vendor discount
options.c: The run-rate should be based on the best single week
options.d: Run-rate is not realized gain; report the two separately

explanation: Counting rules separate run-rate from realized gains. Annualizing three good months and calling it this year's savings overstates what finance will see.
author: claude

stem: The gains case shows €1M saved but leaves out €300K of software and integration costs. What does finance expect?

options.a: Gains shown net of the cost to achieve them
options.b: Gains shown gross, with costs left to the IT budget
options.c: Costs shown only in the year the project ends
options.d: Gains rounded up to offset the missing costs

explanation: Counting rules distinguish gross from net of the cost to achieve. Finance expects the net figure, here €700K, not gross savings with costs parked elsewhere.
author: claude

stem: When should the baseline be agreed with the plant controller?

options.a: Once the pilot shows promising early results
options.b: In week 1, before any software runs
options.c: At go-live, when the first real data arrives
options.d: At year end, when the accounts are closed

explanation: The baseline is co-built with the controller in week 1, before any software runs. Agreed later, it is negotiated around results and gains leak before go-live.
author: claude

stem: At the start of a deployment, what do you agree in writing with the controller?

options.a: The model choice, the hosting and the licence terms
options.b: The target gain and the bonus the project team earns if it is reached
options.c: Metric, formula, data source, normalization and sign-off rule
options.d: The go-live date, the training plan and the user list

explanation: The finance protocol fixes in writing the metric, formula, data source, normalization, review cadence and sign-off threshold, so the gain is not argued afterwards.
author: claude

stem: Your team and the controller compute slightly different gains for the quarter. Which figure gets announced?

options.a: The project team's, since it knows the tool best
options.b: The average of the two, to be fair to both sides
options.c: The controller's, from finance's own spreadsheet
options.d: The higher of the two, if the team can justify it

explanation: The gain is announced by finance's spreadsheet, not yours. Differences go back to the agreed formula, not into a compromise figure.
author: claude

stem: Who should own the capture of gains after go-live?

options.a: The FDE team that built and deployed the tool
options.b: A client-side owner with a mandate over the decisions
options.c: The vendor's customer success manager for the account
options.d: The IT department that runs the system day to day

explanation: Capture needs an owner on the client side with a formal mandate on the gains and authority over the decisions behind them. Builders and IT cannot take those decisions.
author: claude

stem: Alex is named gains owner but cannot change shift patterns or overtime rules. Why is capture at risk?

options.a: Alex should have been chosen from the project team that built the tool
options.b: Shift patterns have little to do with captured gains
options.c: Gains owners should report to IT rather than operations
options.d: Alex lacks the authority to take the decisions behind the gains

explanation: A gains owner needs a formal mandate and the authority to take the decisions behind the gains. A title without that authority leaves freed capacity unconverted.
author: claude

stem: The tool proposes better sequences, but supervisors keep scheduling the old way. Where is value leaking?

options.a: Before go-live, through a baseline nobody agreed
options.b: In the numbers, as KPIs and claims drift apart
options.c: On the floor, as decisions still run on habit
options.d: In the model, through errors in its sequencing

explanation: Gains leak before go-live, on the floor and in the numbers. Here the tool works but decisions still follow habit, so the gain never reaches the P&L.
author: claude

stem: Long changeovers once limited Polymex Industries to two product launches a year. The tool removed that constraint. What follows?

options.a: Reopen the two-launch rule, since its constraint is gone
options.b: Keep the rule, as it is part of the operating plan
options.c: Wait several years before reviewing any of the plant's planning rules
options.d: Count the removed constraint as an immediate gain

explanation: Operating parameters treated as fixed should be reopened once the constraint behind them is gone. Removing the constraint is not yet a gain; using it is.
author: claude

stem: Replanning used to take a day, so the plant reschedules weekly. The tool now replans in minutes. What should the manager do?

options.a: Keep the weekly cadence, since the floor is used to it
options.b: Revisit the weekly cadence, set when replanning was slow
options.c: Replan every few minutes, whenever the tool allows it
options.d: Report the minutes saved per replan as the project gain

explanation: Rescheduling cadence is a parameter set by an old constraint. Once replanning is fast, reopen it; replanning constantly would unsettle the floor.
author: claude

stem: Sold-out plant. A tool frees 2,000 bottleneck hours a year, but the backlog absorbs only 500 more. At €200 contribution per hour, how much is valued at contribution margin?
explanation: Contribution margin applies only to sellable hours, capped by the backlog: 500 × €200 = €100K. €400K values all 2,000 hours as if they could be sold.
author: claude

stem: Plant not sold out. A tool frees 1,000 machine hours. Variable cost €40 per hour, full cost €150, contribution €120. Absent any structural decision, what are they worth?
explanation: When freed hours cannot be sold, they are worth avoided variable cost: 1,000 × €40 = €40K. Full cost and contribution margin overstate the gain.
author: claude

stem: In a sold-out plant, a tool frees hours on a machine that is not the bottleneck. How should those hours be valued?

options.a: At contribution margin, since the plant is sold out
options.b: At full cost per hour, including the overheads
options.c: At most at avoided variable cost, as output cannot rise
options.d: At the bottleneck's hourly rate, since all hours are alike

explanation: Freed capacity is worth contribution margin only when it becomes sellable output. Off the bottleneck, plant output does not rise, so at most variable cost is avoided.
author: claude

stem: Your gains case values freed hours at full cost per hour, overheads included. Why will finance reject it?

options.a: Full cost must first be adjusted for inflation
options.b: Freed hours should be valued at list price instead
options.c: Only direct labor cost can be counted in a gains case
options.d: Overheads do not fall when machine hours are freed

explanation: Valuing freed hours at full cost is a classic error: overheads stay. Value at contribution margin when sellable, otherwise at avoided variable cost.
author: claude

stem: Six months in, the order backlog has shrunk and no longer absorbs all freed hours. What happens to the capacity valuation?

options.a: Hours beyond the backlog drop to avoided variable cost
options.b: Nothing, since the valuation was fixed and signed off at go-live
options.c: All freed hours drop to zero value from that point
options.d: The plant should now value the hours at full cost

explanation: Contribution margin is capped by the order backlog. Hours that can no longer be sold are worth avoided variable cost, so the case must be revalued.
author: claude

stem: What marks a strong gains case, under the course's base, low and high case rule?

options.a: Its high case is at least double its base case
options.b: It still holds up in its own low case
options.c: Its base case matches the vendor's benchmark
options.d: Its figures come from a single, simple case

explanation: Base, low and high cases name the driving assumption, and a strong case survives its own low case. A wide upside proves nothing about robustness.
author: claude

stem: You present base, low and high cases to the CFO. What must each case make explicit?

options.a: The vendor's guarantee behind each figure
options.b: The names of the people who built each case
options.c: The software cost alone, since gains are uncertain
options.d: The driving assumption that moves the result

explanation: Each scenario names its driving assumption, so finance can judge which belief the result rests on and test it.
author: claude

stem: Your base case is strong but the low case shows a net loss. What should you do before the steering committee?

options.a: Present only the base case to keep the message simple
options.b: Average the three cases and present that single figure to the committee
options.c: Treat the case as fragile and rework scope or the key assumption
options.d: Drop the low case as unrealistically pessimistic

explanation: A strong case survives its own low case. A loss in the low case means the result hangs on one assumption; hiding or averaging it misleads finance.
author: claude

stem: Your result swings mostly with how much extra volume sales can place. How should low and high cases be built?

options.a: Vary that volume assumption and name it as the driver
options.b: Apply plus or minus 10% to the final figure for each of the two cases
options.c: Vary the software cost, which is easiest to estimate
options.d: Move every input by the same percentage at once

explanation: Low and high cases flex the driving assumption and name it. A flat percentage on the total hides what the result actually depends on.
author: claude

stem: Bottom-up hours × rates gives €2M a year; top-down from the P&L gives €1.8M. What next?

options.a: Find the error first, since the methods disagree
options.b: Present only the higher figure, since it is more detailed
options.c: Present it: the two methods agree closely enough
options.d: Build a third estimate before showing anything

explanation: When two independent estimates land within 20 to 30% of each other, present the number. A 10% gap is well inside that range.
author: claude

stem: Your bottom-up estimate is €3M a year; the top-down estimate from the P&L is €1M. What do you do?

options.a: Present the average of €2M as a compromise
options.b: Present the bottom-up figure, as it is more detailed
options.c: Present both and let finance choose between them
options.d: Find the error before presenting any figure

explanation: Triangulated estimates should agree within 20 to 30%. A threefold gap means one method is wrong; averaging just hides the error.
author: claude

stem: What does triangulating a gains estimate mean?

options.a: Asking three people from finance to check the same spreadsheet
options.b: Building the same number a second, independent way
options.c: Presenting base, low and high cases side by side
options.d: Comparing the estimate with a vendor's benchmark

explanation: Triangulation rebuilds the number independently, for example top-down from the P&L against bottom-up hours × rates. Scenarios test assumptions, not the method.
author: claude

stem: Two estimates of the gain agree within 5%, but both start from the same hours-saved figure. Why is that weak?

options.a: They are not independent, so agreement proves little
options.b: A 5% gap is too close, since real estimates always differ by more
options.c: Hours saved should never be used in a gains case
options.d: Finance accepts only top-down estimates of gains

explanation: Triangulation needs a second, independent route to the number. Two methods sharing the same key input repeat its error rather than test it.
author: claude

stem: One-time cost €300K. Net gains run at €50K a month for the first two months of ramp, then €100K a month. Payback?

options.a: 2 months
options.b: 3 months
options.c: 4 months
options.d: 6 months

explanation: The ramp yields €100K in two months; the remaining €200K takes two more at €100K, so payback is 4 months. Ignoring the ramp gives 3.
author: claude

stem: Your payback divides one-time cost by the full run-rate from day one. What does this miss?

options.a: The vendor's discount on the second year
options.b: The full cost of the plant's overheads
options.c: The yearly depreciation of the plant's existing machines and tooling
options.d: The ramp: months of lower gains before steady state

explanation: Payback is one-time cost ÷ monthly net run-rate, including the ramp. Assuming full run-rate from day one flatters it.
author: claude

stem: A tool costs €360K one-time plus €30K a month to run, and saves €90K a month from day one. Payback?

options.a: 4 months
options.b: 6 months
options.c: 9 months
options.d: 12 months

explanation: Payback uses the net run-rate: €90K − €30K = €60K a month, so €360K ÷ €60K = 6 months. Four months forgets the running cost.
author: claude

stem: A pilot on the plant's newest, best-run line shows a 25% gain. How should you extrapolate to the whole site?

options.a: Apply 25% to every line, as the pilot proved it
options.b: Raise it, since older lines have more room to improve
options.c: Discount it: pilot lines are rarely representative
options.d: Wait for the vendor to publish a site-wide figure

explanation: Pilot machines are rarely representative. Results from the best-run line need adjusting for the conditions of the other lines before they size a rollout.
author: claude

stem: Why do pilot results often overstate what a rollout will deliver?

options.a: Models lose accuracy as more users join the system
options.b: Pilot machines are picked for good data and keen teams
options.c: Rollouts usually run on a cheaper, less capable version of the tool
options.d: Finance applies looser rules to pilots than to plants

explanation: Pilot selection bias: pilots go where data is clean and teams are willing, so they are rarely representative of the machines a rollout reaches.
author: claude

stem: Sam must pick machines for a pilot whose results will size a rollout case. What keeps the case honest?

options.a: Include typical machines, not only the best documented
options.b: Choose the best machines, to prove what the tool can do at its best
options.c: Choose the worst machines, to show the largest gain
options.d: Let the vendor choose, as it knows the tool best

explanation: Pilot machines are rarely representative, so a pilot that sizes a rollout should include typical machines. Best-case or worst-case picks both bias the number.
author: claude

stem: A tool cuts scrap of purchased raw material. Which line of the P&L improves first?

options.a: Revenue, through higher selling prices
options.b: Inventory, as a one-time cash release
options.c: Sales and admin overheads, below gross margin
options.d: Cost of goods sold, lifting gross margin

explanation: Material lost as scrap is part of cost of goods sold, so less scrap lowers it and raises gross margin. Inventory sits on the balance sheet, not the P&L.
author: claude

stem: Fewer invoice disputes mean customers pay 20 days sooner. How does this show up in the gains case?

options.a: A recurring yearly saving equal to the receivables drop
options.b: Higher revenue in the year of go-live
options.c: Lower receivables: mainly a one-time cash release
options.d: Lower cost of goods sold from next year

explanation: Receivables are working capital. Collecting sooner releases cash once; only the financing cost saved recurs.
author: claude

stem: A line delivers the same output in 500 fewer hours. Which cost actually falls?

options.a: Depreciation charged each year on the line's machines and tooling
options.b: Energy and consumables used per running hour
options.c: The plant manager's salary
options.d: Rent on the plant building

explanation: Fewer running hours cut variable costs such as energy and consumables. Depreciation, salaries and rent are fixed and stay unless a structural decision is taken.
author: claude

stem: What separates gross margin from EBITDA?

options.a: Gross margin already deducts interest and taxes for the year
options.b: EBITDA leaves out cost of goods sold entirely
options.c: They are the same figure under two different names
options.d: EBITDA also deducts operating overheads such as sales and admin

explanation: Gross margin is revenue minus cost of goods sold. EBITDA further deducts operating overheads, before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization.
author: claude

stem: How is contribution margin per unit calculated?

options.a: Price minus variable cost per unit
options.b: Price minus full cost, overheads included
options.c: Revenue minus EBITDA, divided by volume
options.d: Variable cost plus a share of fixed cost

explanation: Contribution margin is price minus variable cost: what each extra unit adds to cover fixed costs and profit. Deducting overheads gives a full-cost margin instead.
author: claude

stem: Last year a line used 25,000 MWh for 12,500 tonnes. This year it used 18,000 MWh for 10,000 tonnes. Volume-normalized saving?
explanation: Baseline rate 2 MWh per tonne × 10,000 tonnes = 20,000 MWh normalized; 20,000 − 18,000 = 2,000 MWh. 7,000 counts the volume drop as a gain.
author: claude

stem: The product mix shifted toward a family with long cycle times. Why normalize the baseline per family rather than plant-wide?

options.a: Finance accepts figures only at the level of each individual product family
options.b: Plant-wide figures are too large for finance to audit
options.c: A plant-wide rate hides shifts between families with different rates
options.d: Per-family figures nearly always show a larger gain

explanation: Normalized baseline = baseline rate × actual volume, per product family. One plant-wide rate turns a mix shift into a false gain or a false loss.
author: claude

stem: Baseline cost per unit: family A €10, family B €20. This year: 1,000 A and 500 B, at a total cost of €18,000. Normalized gain?
explanation: Normalized baseline: 1,000 × €10 + 500 × €20 = €20,000, against €18,000 actual, a €2,000 gain. €4,500 wrongly uses a €15 average rate.
author: claude

stem: A product family launched after go-live has no baseline rate. How should its results enter the gains claim?

options.a: Use the plant-wide average rate of all other families as its baseline
options.b: Count all of its output as gain, since it is new
options.c: Use its rate in the first month after launch
options.d: Leave it out unless finance agrees a rate in writing

explanation: The baseline covers a frozen, named perimeter agreed with finance. A family without a baseline rate stays outside the claim until the controller agrees one.
author: claude

stem: Volume rose 20% after go-live and total cost rose 10%. The plant says costs went up, so the tool has no gain. What is right?

options.a: Agree: costs rose, so there is no gain to claim
options.b: Compare with last year's total cost, unadjusted for volume or mix
options.c: Compare cost with baseline rate × actual volume, per family
options.d: Exclude the year, since volume changed too much

explanation: Normalize: cost should be compared with baseline rate × actual volume, per family. Here cost grew less than volume, which can reveal a real gain.
author: claude

stem: Using the tool's data, procurement wins a one-off €200K rebate from a supplier. How is it counted?

options.a: Once, as a one-time gain, not as an annual saving
options.b: As €200K of savings every year from now on
options.c: Spread as €40K a year over five years
options.d: Not at all, since procurement negotiated it

explanation: Counting rules separate recurring from one-time gains. A one-off rebate counts once; presenting it as annual savings overstates the case.
author: claude

stem: Your bottom-up case puts 70% of the value in direct labor savings. What should you check first?

options.a: Nothing more, since labor is normally the main source of value
options.b: Whether working capital, speed, quality or capex gains were missed
options.c: Whether more headcount could be cut to raise the total
options.d: Whether the labor rates include enough of the plant's overhead

explanation: Direct labor is usually at most about a quarter of the value. A labor-heavy case has probably missed working capital, speed to revenue, quality or deferred capex.
author: claude

stem: Your scheduler frees 1,500 bottleneck hours a year in a sold-out plant. Sales confirms orders for 600 of them. How do you value the other 900?

options.a: At contribution margin, since the plant is sold out today
options.b: At the plant's full cost per hour, since the capacity is real
options.c: At avoided variable cost, unless management takes a structural decision
options.d: At contribution margin, discounted by half for uncertainty

explanation: Contribution margin applies only to hours that sales can fill, capped by the order backlog. Hours beyond it are worth avoided variable cost, or a structural move such as closing a shift, which management decides.
author: claude

stem: A plant runs at 64% of capacity. Your tool frees 2,000 hours on one line. The plant manager asks what they are worth. What is the honest answer?

options.a: Their contribution margin, since output could now rise
options.b: Only the overtime, energy or outsourcing they avoid, or a shift closed
options.c: Their full cost per hour, since fixed costs now spread over fewer running hours
options.d: Nothing at all, because freed hours never reach the P&L

explanation: With spare capacity and flat demand, nobody buys the extra output. Freed hours are worth the variable cost they avoid, or a structural decision management takes. Zero is too strong: avoided overtime is real money.
author: claude

stem: Late deliveries are costing the plant orders, and your tool lifts on-time delivery. What must you have before counting the contribution of orders kept?

options.a: A customer survey showing satisfaction is rising
options.b: On-time delivery held above 95% for a full quarter, as measured by the plant
options.c: The plant manager's estimate of the volume at risk
options.d: Sales naming the orders at risk, backed by contracts or emails

explanation: Revenue protection carries the heaviest burden of proof: finance counts it only when sales names the orders, with contractual or written evidence. A better service level alone proves no euro was kept.
author: claude

stem: Sales says two accounts would take 6% more volume with shorter lead times, but nothing is in writing. How should your gains case treat that volume?

options.a: Outside the base case, as an assumption sales must confirm by a date
options.b: In the base case, since the sales director said it out loud
options.c: As validated revenue, from the day lead times start to fall
options.d: Left out entirely, and not mentioned to the sponsor at all

explanation: An unconfirmed sale is an assumption: log it with an owner and a date, and keep it out of the base case until sales confirms it. Hiding it loses a real upside; counting it now overstates the case.
author: claude

stem: Your low and high cases are simply the base case minus and plus 10%. The CFO is not convinced. Why?

options.a: The range should be wider, about 25%, to look prudent
options.b: Each case should move one named assumption, not a fixed margin
options.c: The high case should already include the rollout to other sites
options.d: A CFO wants one number, so ranges only create confusion

explanation: Low, base and high cases are each driven by a named assumption, such as volume sales can place or the gain on typical machines. A symmetric margin shows no understanding of what moves the result.
author: claude

stem: Your cost-out case still pays if the pilot gain halves. Your capacity case turns negative if demand softens. Which do you lead with at the steering committee?

options.a: The capacity case, since its base case is the larger one
options.b: The sum of the two, presented as one program figure
options.c: Neither, until both have run for a full year on site
options.d: The cost-out case, since it survives its own low case

explanation: A strong case survives its own low case. The capacity case depends on demand that may not come, so it is a condition to state, not the headline. Waiting a year forfeits a case that already holds.
author: claude

stem: Planners say yield on the problem families is 'about 20% lower', but nobody measures it. Your sizing rests on that gap. What do you do?

options.a: Use 20% in the base case, since the planners know the floor
options.b: Drop the yield effect and size only the changeover hours
options.c: Measure it early, and until then treat it as a named range
options.d: Use the ERP's standard rates, which the controller trusts

explanation: An estimate nobody has measured is an assumption: carry it as a range, name it as a driver, and plan how to measure it. Saying what you do not know, and how you will find out, is what a steering committee expects.
author: claude

stem: Bottom-up, hours freed × contribution gives €1.2M a year. Top-down, the share of the P&L line the lever can touch gives €1.0M. What next?

options.a: Present it, showing both paths and the gap between them
options.b: Average the two and present €1.1M as the single figure
options.c: Keep working on both paths until the two agree within about 5%
options.d: Present the bottom-up figure, as it is more detailed

explanation: Two independent paths within 20 to 30% of each other support the order of magnitude, so present it and show both. Chasing a 5% match wastes time; averaging hides the method.
author: claude

stem: Your case is hours saved × contribution per hour. Which second estimate is a real triangulation?

options.a: The same hours saved, recomputed with the controller's own hourly rates
options.b: The pilot result on three machines, scaled to the whole site
options.c: A vendor benchmark of gains at plants of a similar size
options.d: Top-down: the share of the affected P&L line the lever can move

explanation: Triangulation builds the number a second, independent way. Reusing the same hours with other rates repeats the first path's main assumption, so agreement would prove little.
author: claude

stem: One-time cost €200K. Net gains run at €25K a month for the first four months, then €50K a month. What is the payback?

options.a: 4 months
options.b: 5 months
options.c: 6 months
options.d: 8 months

explanation: Four ramp months return €100K; the remaining €100K takes two months at €50K, so 6 months. Dividing by the full run-rate gives 4 and ignores the ramp.
author: claude

stem: In month four, gains run at €40K a month. The sponsor wants to tell the board 'about €480K this year'. What do you advise?

options.a: Fine, as long as finance signed the month-four figure
options.b: Fine, since annualizing a monthly run-rate is common reporting practice
options.c: Report €480K now and correct it at the year-end close
options.d: Call €480K a run-rate, and report what is realized separately

explanation: €40K × 12 is a run-rate, not this year's gain: the months before go-live and the ramp earned less. Run-rate and realized are always stated separately, even when the monthly figure is signed.
author: claude

stem: Your net gain deducts the software and your team's fees. The controller says the figure is still not net. What did you most likely leave out?

options.a: The depreciation of the machines that the new tool now schedules
options.b: The time the client's own people spend on the project
options.c: The revenue lost while the system was being deployed
options.d: The vendor's margin built into the software price

explanation: The cost to achieve covers software, the deployment and the client's time: planners, IT and the controller. Depreciation of existing machines does not change with the project.
author: claude

stem: Your pilot ran on the three machines with the best data and the keenest crew. The rollout covers 14 machines. How do you size the rollout?

options.a: Scale the pilot gain to all 14 machines, exactly as measured
options.b: Discount the pilot gain and make it the low case's driver
options.c: Repeat the pilot on the same three machines to confirm it first
options.d: Replace the pilot result with a vendor's average gain

explanation: Pilot machines are chosen for clean data and keen teams, so they are rarely representative. Discount the gain for typical machines and name it as the assumption that drives the range.
source: Doctrine, value, ROI, validated gains and capture
author: claude

stem: Your case shows €1M of stock reduction plus €200K a year of carrying cost saved, summed as €1.2M a year. What is wrong?

options.a: Carrying cost should not count, since stock is not on the P&L
options.b: Stock reduction should be spread over five years as savings
options.c: The cash comes once; only the carrying cost recurs each year
options.d: Nothing, if the controller agrees the carrying-cost rate

explanation: Inventory releases cash once, in the year stock goes down, and saves carrying cost every year after. Adding the two into one annual figure counts the same euros twice.
author: claude

stem: Your case values fewer changeover hours at contribution margin, and separately adds the overtime those changeovers used to cause. What will the controller say?

options.a: The overtime is a symptom of the changeovers: count it once
options.b: The overtime belongs in the case, as a cost-out line
options.c: The changeover hours should be valued at full cost instead
options.d: The two lines stand, as long as each one is normalized for volume and mix

explanation: Overtime is usually a symptom of changeovers and late plans. Counting both the freed hours and the overtime they caused adds the same euro twice; choose one valuation through the demand fork.
author: claude

stem: Price €1,700 a tonne, variable cost €1,300, full cost €1,600. A sold-out line makes 1,000 more tonnes that sales has placed. What are they worth?
explanation: A tonne is worth its contribution margin: €1,700 − €1,300 = €400 × 1,000 = €400K. Price minus full cost gives €100K and wrongly charges fixed costs that do not move with volume.
author: claude

stem: At a plant with flat demand, the manager says higher OEE will cut cost per tonne and so lift EBIT. What is your view?

options.a: Right: a lower cost per tonne always reaches EBIT within the same year
options.b: Right, provided the OEE gain is measured on the bottleneck line
options.c: A paper gain only, unless the extra output sells or cash costs fall
options.d: Wrong: OEE has no link with cost, only with delivery

explanation: Depreciation and salaried staff do not move when machines run longer. Spreading them over more unsold tonnes lowers unit cost on paper without changing EBIT; money comes from sales or avoided variable cost.
author: claude

stem: Your baseline period includes a week when a line was down for planned maintenance. What should the validation protocol say?

options.a: Nothing: such weeks average out over the baseline period
options.b: The rule for such weeks, written before any result is known
options.c: That the FDE team decides each such week case by case
options.d: That such weeks are dropped whenever they happen to lower the gain

explanation: The controller must run the protocol without you, including what to do with abnormal weeks. A rule fixed in advance stops anyone choosing exclusions after seeing the result.
author: claude

stem: Mix moved toward a family that costs twice as much per tonne. Plant-wide cost per tonne rose 5%, and the plant manager says the tool failed. What do you do?

options.a: Accept it: cost per tonne is the metric the plant reports
options.b: Recompute the baseline as each family's rate × actual volume
options.c: Remove the expensive family from the perimeter after the fact
options.d: Compare against the best month of the baseline year, when the mix was similar

explanation: A plant-wide rate hides shifts between families with different rates. The normalized baseline is baseline rate × actual volume, per family; changing the perimeter afterwards breaks baseline discipline.
source: Doctrine, value, ROI, validated gains and capture
author: claude

stem: Your pipeline gives cleaner output data than the ERP export finance uses today. Which should the baseline use?

options.a: Your pipeline, since its data quality is higher
options.b: An average of the two sources, so that neither side can dispute it
options.c: The system finance already trusts, with its gaps written down
options.d: Whichever source shows the more conservative baseline

explanation: The baseline uses the system finance already trusts, owned by the client, with its known gaps documented in the protocol. A gain built on your own pipeline is one the controller cannot compute without you.
author: claude

stem: Another team's Verifier, playing the controller, cannot tell from your protocol which file to open or who sends it. What does that show?

options.a: The protocol is not finished: it must run without you
options.b: The Verifier needs a short briefing from your team first
options.c: The file name belongs in the steering deck, not the protocol
options.d: The detail can wait until the first monthly review

explanation: A gain exists when the client's controller computes it without you. If the protocol does not say which file, from whom, it fails the controller test; a briefing only hides the gap.
author: claude

stem: Your protocol says the gain becomes official 'once results are consistently good'. What should the sign-off trigger say instead?

options.a: That the sponsor approves each monthly figure in writing
options.b: A confidence interval computed from your team's model
options.c: A fixed date after which the gain is assumed to hold
options.d: A value, and how long it must hold, such as three months

explanation: The sign-off trigger is a value and a duration agreed in week one, so the controller knows exactly which number, held how long, makes it official. Sponsor approval is not finance validation.
author: claude

stem: The group controller says: 'I have never seen a scheduling gain I could find in my numbers.' What is your first move?

options.a: Show the gains other clients reached with similar tools
options.b: Ask the sponsor to overrule the controller on the gain
options.c: Send weekly reports from the tool, so that the gain becomes visible to finance
options.d: Build the baseline and formula with the controller, from their data

explanation: The controller's doubt is the requirement: co-build the baseline, formula and sign-off rule in week one, from the data finance trusts. Reports from your own tool are exactly what was never found in the numbers.
author: claude

stem: Your scheduling project pushes on-time delivery. Which measure is a guardrail on its scorecard?

options.a: Plans published from the system each week
options.b: Scrap and changeovers per shift
options.c: Answer time to a customer's change request
options.d: Quoted lead time on new orders

explanation: A guardrail is what must not get worse while you push the outcome: on-time delivery bought with extra changeovers is paid in scrap. Plans published is adoption; answer time is a driver; lead time is an outcome.
source: Day 3, from the stated process to the target architecture
author: claude

stem: The team proposes 'parser accuracy above 98%' as the project's headline success measure. What is wrong with it?

options.a: It describes the system, not what the plant or customer notices
options.b: 98% is too low a bar for a parser running in production
options.c: It should be computed by the controller, not by the team
options.d: Accuracy should be measured on a sample, not on every message

explanation: Good is defined by what the client would notice. Parser accuracy belongs in the eval set; the headline measure is an outcome such as on-time delivery or quoted lead time.
source: Day 3, from the stated process to the target architecture
author: claude

stem: Baseline on-time delivery is 84%; the best week last quarter was 91%; the solver says a perfect plan gives 97%. Where should the target sit?

options.a: At 86%, two points above the baseline, to be safe
options.b: At 91%, since the best week proves it can be done
options.c: Between 91% and 97%, with a date and an owner
options.d: At 97%, since the solver proves it is reachable

explanation: The target sits between best demonstrated and entitlement, with a number, a date and an owner. Entitlement assumes a perfect plan; two points over baseline may be lost in weekly noise.
source: Day 3, from the stated process to the target architecture
author: claude

stem: Weekly on-time delivery moves about two points with nothing changing. The draft charter promises one point of improvement. What do you change?

options.a: Nothing: one point a week adds up over a year
options.b: Measure monthly instead, so that the weekly noise disappears from view
options.c: Aim higher, or measure something closer to the cause
options.d: Ask the controller to smooth the weekly figures

explanation: A gain smaller than the weekly noise cannot be seen, so nobody can sign it. Size the target above the noise, or pick a driver measure closer to the cause that moves visibly.
source: Day 3, from the stated process to the target architecture
author: claude

stem: Week 6: you find the scrap baseline counts regrind twice, so the gain shown to the CFO is a third too high. Steering is on Friday. What do you do?

options.a: Tell the sponsor and controller within a day, with the corrected figure
options.b: Correct it quietly in the next monthly report
options.c: Wait for Friday and present the correction to the whole committee
options.d: Keep the figure, since the trend in scrap is still right

explanation: Announce the error first, with the corrected number and what it changes. Trust lost by a correction comes back; trust lost by a cover-up does not. Waiting for Friday lets the CFO hear it in a meeting.
source: Day 4, what goes wrong, and how it scales
author: claude

stem: You bring the planning system to a second plant running at 64% of capacity. Its planner shows no interest. What is the likely reason?

options.a: She has not yet seen the gains measured at the first plant
options.b: She needs more training on the system before she adopts it
options.c: She wins little from a better plan when lines are half empty
options.d: Her plant manager has not yet made use of the system mandatory for her

explanation: Each actor must be able to say what they win. In a plant short of orders a better plan moves little, so the first plant's product may be the wrong first product there; start from that plant's own problem.
source: Day 4, what goes wrong, and how it scales
author: claude

stem: The group COO wants one gain figure for the four-plant rollout, computed by your central team. What do you propose?

options.a: One figure, computed centrally with a shared group method
options.b: The first plant's gain, multiplied by the number of plants
options.c: A group figure from the ERP, signed by the group CFO alone
options.d: Gains each plant's controller measures, then added up

explanation: What counts as a gain belongs to the controller, and each plant has its own baseline and perimeter. The COO gets gains a controller can measure plant by plant; a central figure is the team's model again.
source: Day 4, what goes wrong, and how it scales
author: claude

stem: Your kickoff document for the client's executive committee has a target, scope and roles. What must it also set for each gate?

options.a: A measurable condition that stops the project, agreed now
options.b: A budget reserve to extend the phase if it runs late
options.c: The list of features the team will deliver by the end of that phase
options.d: The user satisfaction score the phase should reach

explanation: Kill criteria are written on day one, one per gate, while nobody is attached to the solution yet. About 30% of initiatives fail; a stop at a gate keeps the account, a zombie project loses it.
author: claude

stem: At week 4, the backtest shows changeovers explain a fifth of the delivery loss; the charter's kill criterion said a third. The sponsor wants to go on. What do you do?

options.a: Extend the phase by four more weeks, to gather more data on the losses
options.b: Lower the threshold, since a fifth is still material
options.c: Continue, and raise it at the next steering committee
options.d: Take the stop to the steering committee, written up as a result

explanation: The kill criterion was agreed before anyone was attached, so it holds. A kill is a result: write it up and send it to the controller like a gain. Moving the threshold after the fact empties the charter.
author: claude

stem: A use case would save €150K a year; capturing it costs €100K a year in software and people. The sponsor likes it. What do you advise?

options.a: Look elsewhere: it is not worth ten times its cost
options.b: Go ahead, but only after a pilot on the best line
options.c: Go ahead, since the net gain is positive from year one
options.d: Go ahead if the vendor cuts the software price

explanation: A problem worth solving is worth at least ten times what it costs to capture. A thin positive margin disappears with the first delay or the low case, and leaves no room for the change it demands.
author: claude
